title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks

paper.title: Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks
paper.abstract:
Abstract Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge — and when they improve generalization — is challenging, since training is nonlinear and nonconvex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer’s feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth.
We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that
KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization — an “anti-shrinkage” mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters — notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment.
Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: A defining trait of deep neural networks is their ability to learn data-dependent features within their internal layers [ 1 ] . This ability marks a salient departure from their predecessors — kernel models — which utilize a fixed set of features and only learn how to weight them: z ⁡ ( x , θ ) = ∑ j = 1 N W j ​ ϕ j ​ ( x ) z(x;\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_{j}\phi_{j}(x) (1.1) Here, θ = ( W 1 , W 2 , … , W N ) \theta=(W_{1},W_{2},\dots,W_{N}) is a collection of regression weights and ϕ 1 , ϕ 2 , … , ϕ N \phi_{1},\phi_{2},\dots,\phi_{N} are basis functions that transform the input x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} into the features ( ϕ j ​ ( x ) ) 1 ≤ j ≤ N (\phi_{j}(x))_{1\leq j\leq N} , giving rise to a feature map x ↦ ( ϕ 1 ​ ( x ) , … , ϕ N ​ ( x ) ) x\mapsto(\phi_{1}(x),\dots,\phi_{N}(x)) . A kernel model learns the W j W_{j} while holding this map fixed; a deep network additionally adapts the map to the data through training. This process of feature learning is widely credited for the empirical success of deep networks [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , yet it is precisely what places them outside the reach of kernel theory. We therefore ask: what data-dependent features does a deep neural network learn, and when do such features generalize better than fixed, data-independent ones? Answers to these questions are complicated by two issues. First, the learning dynamics of deep neural networks are nonlinear and nonconvex, making closed-form descriptions of feature learning limited. A large body of work addresses this issue by passing to an infinite-width limit ( N → ∞ N\to\infty ), in which aspects of the network dynamics collapse onto deterministic objects. The μ ​ P \mu P [ 6 ] and mean-field [ 7 ] network parameterizations support stable feature learning in this limit, and have been used to analyze the training dynamics and convergence properties of deep networks [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Within these descriptions, the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) [ 12 , 13 ] characterizes the full training trajectory in terms of a reduced set of deterministically evolving kernel order parameters, which include the network’s feature kernels at each layer. This analysis is powerful, but it characterizes feature learning implicitly through self-consistent equations for order parameters, rather than explicitly computing the features learned under gradient descent. Additionally, the DMFT typically involves fixing the training dataset [ 12 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] , leaving open settings in which the number of data points n n and data dimension D D grow in addition to the width N N (which [ 16 ] explores for deep linear networks). Here, n / D → ψ = 0.2 n/D\to\psi=0.2 and the noise level is σ 2 = 1 \sigma^{2}=1 . Blue denotes a feature learning advantage, and red denotes the opposite. The shaded region marks an “SNR window” in which a global feature learning advantage provably holds: certain one-step ridge estimators ( k ℓ > 0 k_{\ell}>0 ) can outperform any baseline ridge estimator (see Sec. 4.3 ). To the right, generalization error curves over λ \lambda are shown for one-step ( k ℓ → 10 k_{\ell}\to 10 ; blue) and baseline (red) estimators for selected values of γ \gamma and the SNR ( ρ 2 / σ 2 \rho^{2}/\sigma^{2} ). A. γ = 0.25 \gamma=0.25 , SNR = 1.0 \text{SNR}=1.0 . B. γ = 20 \gamma=20 , SNR = 0.0049 \text{SNR}=0.0049 . C. γ = 10 \gamma=10 , SNR = 0.25 \text{SNR}=0.25 . See Appendix A for more details. The second issue is that the usefulness of any learned features depends on the underlying data distribution. While prior theoretical approaches often use isotropic inputs [ 1 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] , real-world data often contains low-dimensional structure embedded in otherwise high-dimensional observations [ 21 , 22 ] . A canonical model for studying such structure is a spiked matrix model [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] , in which a rank-one signal is embedded in high-dimensional noise. For regression tasks, this model is governed by two key parameters: the spike strength ( γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 ) of this rank-one signal, and the spike-target alignment ( ρ ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] \rho\in[-1,1] ) between the signal and ground truth regression directions. Altogether, inputs are sampled as x i ​ ∼ iid ​ N ​ ( 0 , I D + γ ​ v ​ v T ) x_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,I_{D}+\gamma vv^{T}) and targets as y i = 1 D ​ w ⋆ T ​ x i + ϵ i y_{i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}w_{\star}^{T}x_{i}+\epsilon_{i} , with ϵ i ​ ∼ iid ​ N ​ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \epsilon_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^{2}) and w ⋆ w_{\star} fixed so that 1 D ​ w ⋆ T ​ v = ρ \frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}w_{\star}^{T}v=\rho . In light of these issues, here we develop a simplified framework for describing feature learning and when it is useful, making three key modeling choices that afford closed-form analysis while preserving the phenomenon of interest. First, we study deep linear networks with L ≥ 1 L\geq 1 layers and width N N , in a mean-field parameterization, for which optimization remains nonlinear, nonconvex, as well as genuinely depth-dependent [ 25 , 26 ] . Second, for a fixed dataset of D D -dimensional inputs X = [ x 1 , … , x n ] ∈ ℝ D × n X=[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times n} and scalar targets y = [ y 1 , … , y n ] ∈ ℝ n y=[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , we take a single gradient descent (GD) step with step size η \eta on the empirical mean squared error loss from initialization. As a result, writing θ t \theta_{t} for the network’s weights after t t steps of GD ( t ∈ { 0 , 1 } t\in\{0,1\} ), this approach allows us to exactly calculate each layer’s feature kernel Φ t ℓ := ( h ℓ ​ ( x i , θ t ) ⋅ h ℓ ​ ( x j , θ t ) N ) 1 ≤ i , j ≤ n ∈ ℝ n × n , 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ L , \Phi^{\ell}_{t}:=\left(\frac{h^{\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{t})\cdot h^{\ell}(x_{j};\theta_{t})}{N}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\hskip 23.49976pt1\leq\ell\leq L, (1.2) in the limit of N → ∞ N\to\infty (with n n and D D fixed), both before and after one step, and to compare it with the baseline input kernel K x := X T ​ X D ∈ ℝ n × n K_{x}:=\frac{X^{T}X}{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} . Here, h ℓ ​ ( x , θ ) ∈ ℝ N h^{\ell}(x;\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{N} denotes the layer- ℓ \ell representation of the input x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . Third, to study when the features given by the limiting layer- ℓ \ell one-step feature kernel are useful, we sample data from a spiked matrix model and subsequently take n , D → ∞ n,D\to\infty ; this enables us to compute (in closed-form) the generalization error arising from these features under kernel ridge regression (for any ridge strength λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 ) in the overparameterized proportional limit n / D → ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) n/D\to\psi\in(0,1) , and to identify settings of γ \gamma and ρ \rho that lead to better generalization after one step. Together, these choices allow us to discover how one gradient step updates the layer- ℓ \ell feature kernel, how this change propagates to the resulting kernel ridge estimator, and for which data distributions this update lowers the generalization error. Ultimately, we find that one gradient step within a deep linear network causes each of its layers to acquire a target-aligned low-rank spike, setting it up to improve generalization for data distributions with target-aligned low-dimensional structure (i.e. γ \gamma and ρ 2 / σ 2 \rho^{2}/\sigma^{2} are sufficiently large), and to fail to do so if this structure is missing (Fig. 1 ). Our approach is reminiscent of the one-step analysis of Ba et al. (2022) [ 19 ] , in which one gradient step in a nonlinear network with one hidden layer ( L = 1 L=1 ) causes the first-layer weights to acquire a target-aligned rank-one spike. Moreover, ridge regression on the updated hidden-state activations leads to meaningful improvement in generalization for a sufficiently large step. We find similar results in our work (see our contributions below). Unlike Ba et al., however, we do not consider nonlinearities. Nonetheless, this simplification precisely allows us to capture (in closed-form) feature learning in deeper networks ( L > 1 ) (L>1) and isolate the role of structure in the data in shaping a generalization advantage.

sections.heading: 1.1 Our Contributions
sections.text: Our core findings and analyses can be summarized as follows.

sections.heading: 3. For data coming from a spiked population model, we derive and analyze closed-form asymptotic formulas for bias, variance, and generalization error.
sections.text: In the proportional limit n / D → ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) n/D\to\psi\in(0,1) and where the task is noisy linear regression ( y i = 1 D w ⋆ T x i + ϵ i , ϵ i ∼ iid N ( 0 , σ 2 ) ) \left(y_{i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}w_{\star}^{T}x_{i}+\epsilon_{i},\text{ }\epsilon_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^{2})\right) , we derive these exact formulas for f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} (Thm. 4.3 ; see Fig. 4 ). We decompose the generalization error into bias , which measures how well the average predictor fits the targets, and variance , which measures the estimator’s sensitivity to the specific dataset. Since all estimators coincide when λ = 0 \lambda=0 , we ask how feature learning affects bias and variance when mild ridge is added (Prop. 4.4 ; Fig. 5 ): (A) To first order in λ \lambda around λ = 0 \lambda=0 , the bias of the baseline estimator f ^ λ ; 0 \hat{f}_{\lambda;0} increases and its variance decreases. (B) To first order in λ \lambda around λ = 0 \lambda=0 , the effect of adding feature learning ( 0 < k ℓ = Θ D ​ ( 1 ) 0<k_{\ell}=\Theta_{D}(1) ) is to decrease the bias (of f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} ) relative to that of f ^ λ ; 0 \hat{f}_{\lambda;0} , and to increase the variance (of f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} ) relative to that of f ^ λ ; 0 \hat{f}_{\lambda;0} . Altogether, ridge and feature learning act as opposing forces along the bias-variance axis. Intuitively, ridge alone shrinks the estimator, increasing bias, but improves robustness to noise in the dataset, decreasing variance. Adding feature learning-induced uniform inflation corrects shrinkage on average at the cost of amplifying noise along task-irrelevant directions. The question is when this bias-for-variance trade is worth making.

sections.heading: 4. A feature learning advantage exists when the data carries a sufficiently strong, target-aligned spike, and vanishes in the absence of a spike or target-alignment
sections.text: (see Fig. 1 ) . As γ \gamma grows the upper bound diverges and the lower bound descends to SNR crit = ψ 2 / ( 1 − ψ ) 2 \mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{crit}}=\psi^{2}/(1-\psi)^{2} , so for a strong enough spike this condition collapses to an SNR lower bound set by the aspect ratio ψ \psi . On the other hand, for isotropic inputs ( γ = 0 \gamma=0 ) or for a task-orthogonal spike ( ρ = 0 \rho=0 ), we prove that no choice of ( λ , k ℓ ) (\lambda,k_{\ell}) beats the optimally tuned baseline ridge estimator (Thm. 4.7 ; see Fig. 7 ). Collectively, these results resemble a deep linear network-based analog of the famous BBP phase transition [ 24 , 27 ] : the “spiked” one-step kernel meaningfully picks up the “spike” in the data once the spike strength and SNR are sufficiently large.

sections.heading: Deep linear networks.
sections.text: Despite their lack of nonlinearities, deep linear networks possess a nonconvex loss landscape [ 28 ] and depth-dependent training dynamics [ 25 , 29 ] , making them an analytically tractable testbed for theories of learning [ 30 , 12 , 31 , 32 ] . Notably, Saxe et al. (2014) [ 25 ] show that when weights are suitably “decoupled”, modes of the input–output correlation are acquired sequentially in order of their singular values, so that depth gives rise to “stage-like” transitions in learning. Closer to our question, Atanasov et al. (2022) [ 33 ] show that at small initialization a deep linear network’s neural tangent kernel (NTK) can align with the target early in training. In a similar vein, we make the earliest such alignment explicit: after a single step, each layer’s feature kernel acquires a target-aligned rank-one component.

sections.heading: One-step analyses.
sections.text: A key approach for explicitly characterizing the features a network acquires is to study the features learned after a single GD step from initialization. For two-layer nonlinear networks, Ba et al. (2022) [ 19 ] show that one GD step imprints a rank-one “spike” on the first-layer weights that aligns with the linear component of the target, and that ridge regression on the resulting features can strictly improve generalization over kernel estimators with no learned features once the step size is large enough. Subsequent work refines this picture: larger learning-rate scalings can imprint multiple spikes, each capturing a higher-order component of the target [ 34 ] ; the one-GD-step network can be mapped to a spiked random features model, for which test error asymptotics may be derived [ 35 ] ; and learning multi-index targets requires characteristic batch sizes and numbers of GD steps [ 20 ] . These analyses treat two-layer nonlinear networks with isotropic inputs, and typically express the generalization error through self-consistent equations that must be solved numerically. In this paper, we study linear networks but account for depth and a particular class of anisotropic inputs, and we carry out our analyses in closed form.

sections.heading: Spiked matrix models.
sections.text: The spiked population model we study stems from Johnstone (2001) [ 23 ] , and its defining feature is the BBP transition [ 24 ] : the top sample eigenvalue separates from the bulk only once the spike strength exceeds a critical value set by the aspect ratio. Using this model, prior work has shown that feature learning can exploit a spike, a property that depends both on the spike strength and the spike-target alignment [ 21 , 22 ] . In this paper, we make this dependence quantitative for a deep linear network.

sections.heading: High-dimensional ridge regression.
sections.text: Ridge regularization classically serves to shrink estimation, mitigating overfitting in order to lower test error [ 36 ] . Using tools from random matrix theory — notably the Marcenko–Pastur law — prior work has derived asymptotics for the generalization error of ridge regression in the proportional regime and characterized the optimal ridge strength [ 37 ] . However, this shrinkage prescription can fail for heavily overparameterized settings ( D ≫ n D\gg n ) in which the population covariance is anisotropic and the true regression direction is aligned with its top eigendirections [ 38 ] . For example, for a spiked covariance, the optimal ridge strength can even be negative [ 39 ] . More recently, Freeman (2025) [ 40 ] shows that scalar inflation of the minimum ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm interpolator ( λ = 0 \lambda=0 ) lowers the generalization error for sufficiently anisotropic covariances when D ≫ n D\gg n . These ideas challenge the classical wisdom that shrinkage enhances prediction, suggesting that inflating estimation can improve test error in certain cases. In this paper, we arrive at inflation from a different angle. Rather than being prescribed, the inflation factor c λ c_{\lambda} is produced by one GD step; in effect, the deep linear network discovers an anti-shrinkage correction on its own.

sections.text: It is a curious fact that f ^ λ ; feat \hat{f}_{\lambda;\feat} is a λ \lambda -dependent inflation of f ^ λ ; init \hat{f}_{\lambda;\init} , given that the role of ridge is to shrink f ^ λ ; init \hat{f}_{\lambda;\init} relative to the unregularized interpolator f ^ 0 ; init \hat{f}_{0;\text{init}} . sections.heading: 4.3 Identifying when a feature learning advantage holds — and when it does not
sections.text: We now turn to analyzing when the one step of feature learning asymptotically attains a lower generalization error than that of any baseline estimator, as well as when it does not. Fixing the “macroscopic” parameters ψ \psi , γ \gamma , ρ \rho , and σ \sigma , the generalization error arising from a given estimator f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} will systematically vary as a function of the ridge strength λ \lambda and the feature learning update strength k ℓ k_{\ell} . Here, we seek to identify the settings (characterized by the value of ψ \psi , σ \sigma , γ \gamma , and ρ \rho ) in which feature learning-based estimation reliably lowers generalization error compared to any baseline estimator: inf λ ≥ 0 , k ℓ > 0 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; k ℓ ) < inf λ ≥ 0 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; 0 ) \inf_{\lambda\geq 0,k_{\ell}>0}\tilde{\mathcal{G}}\left(\hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}}\right)<\inf_{\lambda\geq 0}\tilde{\mathcal{G}}\left(\hat{f}_{\lambda;0}\right) (4.11) When this inequality holds, we will say that there is a global feature learning advantage (FLA). To develop an intuition for when a global FLA holds, we first identify settings in which one step of feature learning results in a lower generalization error locally around λ = 0 \lambda=0 . Interestingly, the sufficient conditions we identify for a local FLA also turn out to be sufficient conditions for a global FLA. In effect, within these settings, the emergence of an FLA locally around λ = 0 \lambda=0 extends to a local FLA around any λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 ; altogether, this results in a global FLA. Finally, we rigorously characterize two key settings in which a global FLA does not hold: the setting of isotropic inputs ( γ = 0 \gamma=0 ) and the setting of a task-orthogonal spike ( ρ = 0 \rho=0 ).

Theorem 4.5 . Suppose that γ > 0 \gamma>0 and σ 2 > 0 \sigma^{2}>0 and that Assumption 1 holds. The upper bound for ρ 2 / σ 2 \rho^{2}/\sigma^{2} in Ineq. 4.18 serves as a way to ensure that 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; 0 ) \tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;0}) does not attain a global minimum at λ = 0 \lambda=0 . sections.heading: 4.3.3 No feature learning advantage in the isotropic setting
sections.text: Figure 7: Comparison of asymptotic generalization error curves over λ \lambda for one-step estimators ( k ℓ = 10 k_{\ell}=10 ) and baseline estimators, shown for a setting where the inputs are isotropic (left) and a setting where the spike and target directions are orthogonal (right). Here, ψ = σ = 0.5 \psi=\sigma=0.5 . Markers represent empirical simulations (with SEM; D = 3000 D=3000 , n = 1500 n=1500 ) and solid lines indicate theory. Stars indicate the minimum generalization error attained by either kernel. Previously, we have shown that when γ \gamma and ρ 2 σ 2 \frac{\rho^{2}}{\sigma^{2}} are each taken to be suitably large, a global FLA holds per Ineq. 4.18 . Notably, this inequality will fail to hold when γ ↓ 0 \gamma\downarrow 0 or ρ = 0 \rho=0 . Here, we rigorously prove that a global FLA fails to hold when γ = 0 \gamma=0 — which corresponds to a setting in which inputs are isotropic (i.e. drawn i.i.d. from N ⁡ ( 0 , I D ) N(0,I_{D}) ) — or when ρ = 0 \rho=0 — which corresponds to a setting in which the spike direction is orthogonal to the target direction. In particular, among all possible combinations of ( λ , k ℓ ) ∈ ℝ ≥ 0 2 (\lambda,k_{\ell})\in\mathbb{R}^{2}_{\geq 0} , we show that there exists a baseline estimator that attains the lowest possible generalization error. Theorem 4.7 . Suppose that γ = 0 \gamma=0 or ρ = 0 \rho=0 , with ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \psi\in(0,1) , and that Assumption 1 holds. Then, if σ 2 > 0 \sigma^{2}>0 , the following results hold: 1. When viewed as a function in λ \lambda , 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; 0 ) \tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;0}) is strictly decreasing for λ ∈ [ 0 , σ 2 ) \lambda\in[0,\sigma^{2}) and strictly increasing for λ ∈ ( σ 2 , ∞ ) \lambda\in(\sigma^{2},\infty) . In particular, inf λ ≥ 0 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; 0 ) = 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ σ 2 ; 0 ) \inf_{\lambda\geq 0}\tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;0})=\tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\sigma^{2};0}) and this minimum is uniquely attained when λ = σ 2 \lambda=\sigma^{2} . 2. For any λ , k ℓ ≥ 0 \lambda,k_{\ell}\geq 0 , 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; k ℓ ) ≥ 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ σ 2 ; 0 ) \tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}})\geq\tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\sigma^{2};0}) with equality if and only if ( λ , k ℓ ) = ( σ 2 , 0 ) (\lambda,k_{\ell})=(\sigma^{2},0) . If γ = 0 \gamma=0 or ρ = 0 \rho=0 in the noiseless regime ( σ 2 = 0 \sigma^{2}=0 ), then 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; 0 ) \tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;0}) strictly increases over λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 , thereby attaining a unique minimum when λ = 0 \lambda=0 . Moreover, inf λ ≥ 0 , k ℓ ≥ 0 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; k ℓ ) = 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ 0 ; 0 ) \inf_{\lambda\geq 0,k_{\ell}\geq 0}\tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}})=\tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{0;0}) , and this minimum is attained if and only if λ = 0 \lambda=0 (with no restrictions on k ℓ k_{\ell} ). A proof of this result is provided in Appendix D.4.5 . Ultimately, whenever γ = 0 \gamma=0 or ρ = 0 \rho=0 , the lowest generalization error comes from a baseline estimator — namely one where the ridge strength is tuned to λ = σ 2 \lambda=\sigma^{2} . Although inflation arising from one step of feature learning could partially undo the shrinkage effects of over-regularization (i.e. for large λ \lambda ), it cannot outperform the optimally tuned ridge-only baseline (see Fig. 7 ). We also remark that the asymptotic generalization error, as given by Eq. 4.6 , is the same regardless of whether γ = 0 \gamma=0 or ρ = 0 \rho=0 , since all of the γ \gamma and ρ \rho dependencies appear together; in this sense, γ \gamma and ρ \rho may be seen as two sides of the same coin. The upshot of Theorem 4.7 is that a feature learning advantage requires a genuine spike that is at least partially aligned with the target direction.

sections.heading: 5 Discussion
sections.text: In this paper, we studied the earliest signatures of feature learning in a deep linear network: the change in the layer- ℓ \ell feature kernel under a single gradient step, the effect of this change on estimators obtained by kernel ridge regression (KRR), as well as the generalization error arising from these estimators under KRR. Three aspects of our analysis are worth emphasizing. First, the effective strength of one step of feature learning is governed by both the learning rate η \eta (as demonstrated by prior works) and the layer index ℓ \ell , highlighting in particular that utilizing depth is another mechanism for increasing the strength of feature learning without needing to scale the learning rate. Second, our work highlights the tension between the uniform inflation arising from one gradient step and the shrinkage arising from ridge regularization, which act as opposing forces along the bias-variance tradeoff; ridge tilts the balance towards lowering variance and inflation tilts the balance towards lowering the bias. Third, we find that a feature learning advantage (at the level of one step) is not possible unless genuine task-relevant low-rank structure is present in the data. This suggests that gradient descent is especially well-suited to learning structured low-dimensional information embedded in otherwise high-dimensional data, even early in training. We now highlight key limitations of our work, alongside important future directions.

sections.heading: Going beyond linearity.
sections.text: Our closed-form analysis is afforded, in part, by the linearity of our deep networks. Carrying out similar analyses with deep nonlinear networks could provide a richer description of the linear and higher-order nonlinear modes of target functions that can be efficiently learned early in training. As a salient point of contrast with our present work, Ba et al. (2022) [ 19 ] find that for two-layer nonlinear networks, features learned under one gradient step can improve generalization in a setting with isotropic inputs, thereby removing the need for low-rank structure in the inputs. Thus, future work would involve characterizing the feature learning advantages (and limitations) that arise from nonlinear computation.

sections.heading: Going beyond one step.
sections.text: An important simplification in our analysis is to study a single step of gradient descent, because it makes the learned feature kernel Φ t ℓ \Phi^{\ell}_{t} exactly computable. Nonetheless, a natural next step is to study how Φ t ℓ \Phi^{\ell}_{t} evolves across several gradient steps, how it depends on learning rate and depth, and how it might further widen the feature learning advantage. Such an analysis would come closer to the long training-time setting studied by Bordelon & Pehlevan (2022) [ 12 ] while providing greater transparency of what features are learned.

sections.heading: Going beyond one spike.
sections.text: Here, we studied data distributions in which the inputs have one “spike” direction. A natural extension is to study data distributions consisting of multiple “spikes”, or in which the target functions are multi-index models [ 20 ] . This would raise new questions as to whether distinct task-relevant directions can be learned within a single gradient step or whether this requires multiple steps.

sections.heading: Studying the predictive power of one gradient step.
sections.text: The main limitation of a one-step analysis is that it omits a description of learning later in training. However, it remains to explore whether the feature learning phenomena observed at the level of one step meaningfully predict longer-term learning behaviors. In particular, establishing a link between early signatures of learning and longer-term generalization error could inform optimal architectural and training paradigms for learning particular data distributions.

sections.heading: AI usage.
sections.text: In carrying out this research, we used AI to help run numerical experiments and generate figures. We also used it to explore possible strategies for proving certain results (e.g. Thm. 3.1 , Thm. 4.7 ). Finally, we used AI to verify the correctness of our proofs and overall prose.

sections.heading: Appendix A Experimental Details
sections.text: All figures presented in the main text were generated using the NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib libraries in Python. All experiments were either run locally or on a high-performance computing cluster composed of CPU nodes supporting serial and parallel workloads. All code will be made publicly available within a GitHub repository upon publication. Here, we present further details of the experiments and analyses used to generate each of the figures in the main text.

sections.heading: A note regarding asymptotic limits.
sections.text: As described in the paper, our methodology is to first take the N → ∞ N\to\infty limit and next to take the n , D → ∞ n,D\to\infty (proportional) limit. Thus, in generating figures other than Fig. 2 (which provides numerical validation for Thm. 3.1 for large, finite N N ), we assume that the N → ∞ N\to\infty limit has already been taken, giving rise to the inflationary constant c λ c_{\lambda} . In these figures, we focus on empirically validating the results we obtain under the second limit, where n / D → ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) n/D\to\psi\in(0,1) and the data is sampled from a spiked population model (as stated in Assumption 1 ).

sections.heading: Generalization error curves (Figs. 1 , 4 , 5 , 7 ).
sections.text: Here, we describe the procedure used to find the location of the minimum asymptotic generalization error over ridge strength ( λ \lambda ), marked as stars in each of the indicated figures in the paper. For any fixed values of ψ \psi , γ \gamma , ρ \rho , σ \sigma , and k ℓ k_{\ell} , we compute the asymptotic generalization error 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; k ℓ ) \tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}}) across m = 200 m=200 values of λ \lambda on a log-spaced grid between 0.001 0.001 and 1000 1000 as well as at λ = 0 \lambda=0 . Based on preliminary exploration, we chose λ = 1000 \lambda=1000 as a reasonable upper bound beyond which we do not expect 𝒢 ~ ​ ( f ^ λ ; k ℓ ) \tilde{\mathcal{G}}(\hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}}) to have a minimum. Write the collection of all of these values of λ \lambda as 0 = λ 0 < λ 1 < ⋯ < λ m = 1000 0=\lambda_{0}<\lambda_{1}<\dots<\lambda_{m}=1000 . We then collect every i ∈ { 0 , 1 , … , m } i\in\{0,1,\dots,m\} such that λ i \lambda_{i} results in a smaller asymptotic generalization error than its immediate neighbors on the grid; we record each such i i because the asymptotic generalization error can be non-monotonic in λ \lambda (e.g. see Fig. 1 B). We also mark the lowest generalization error value attained over these λ i \lambda_{i} . Then, for each of these identified i i , we apply scipy.optimize.minimize_scalar to find the minimum asymptotic generalization error in the range [ λ max ⁡ ( 0 , i − 1 ) , λ min ⁡ ( i + 1 , m ) ] \left[\lambda_{\max(0,i-1)},\lambda_{\min(i+1,m)}\right] . sections.text: Lemma B.1 . (a) Suppose that M ∈ ℝ N × N M\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is a matrix satisfying the following property: for any orthogonal matrix U ∈ ℝ N × N U\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} , the equation M = U ​ M ​ U T M=UMU^{T} holds. Then, M = λ ​ I N M=\lambda I_{N} , for some λ ∈ ℝ \lambda\in\mathbb{R} . (b) Suppose that M ∈ ℝ N × N M\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} is a matrix and v ∈ 𝕊 N − 1 ⊂ ℝ N v\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1}\subset\mathbb{R}^{N} is a unit vector that collectively satisfy the following property: for any orthogonal matrix U ∈ ℝ N × N U\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} that fixes v v (i.e. U ​ v = v Uv=v ), the equation M = U ​ M ​ U T M=UMU^{T} holds. Then, there exist λ 1 , λ 2 ∈ ℝ \lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}\in\mathbb{R} such that M = λ 1 ​ I N + λ 2 ​ v ​ v T M=\lambda_{1}I_{N}+\lambda_{2}vv^{T} . Proof. (a) First, consider any unit vector w ∈ 𝕊 N − 1 w\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1} . Since U ​ M = M ​ U UM=MU for all orthogonal matrices U U , this identity holds for all orthogonal matrices that fix w w . In particular, for any orthogonal matrix U U that fixes w w , we have that M ​ w = M ​ U ​ w = U ​ M ​ w Mw=MUw=UMw , i.e. U U also fixes M ​ w Mw . We claim that M ​ w = λ w ​ w Mw=\lambda_{w}w , for some λ w ∈ ℝ \lambda_{w}\in\mathbb{R} . Indeed, we may first write the decomposition M ​ w = λ w ​ w + w ⟂ Mw=\lambda_{w}w+w_{\perp} , where λ w ∈ ℝ \lambda_{w}\in\mathbb{R} and w ⟂ w_{\perp} is some vector in ( span ​ ( { w } ) ) ⟂ \left(\text{span}(\{w\})\right)^{\perp} . Then, if U ​ M ​ w = M ​ w UMw=Mw for all orthogonal matrices U U that fix w w , we obtain λ w ​ w + w ⟂ = M ​ w = U ​ M ​ w = U ⁡ ( λ w ​ w + w ⟂ ) = λ w ​ w + U ​ w ⟂ . \lambda_{w}w+w_{\perp}=Mw=UMw=U\left(\lambda_{w}w+w_{\perp}\right)=\lambda_{w}w+Uw_{\perp}. This implies that for all orthogonal matrices U U that fix w w , w ⟂ = U ​ w ⟂ w_{\perp}=Uw_{\perp} . If w ⟂ ≠ 0 w_{\perp}\neq 0 , then there exists some orthogonal matrix U 0 U_{0} that fixes w w but does not fix w ⟂ w_{\perp} . Indeed, identifying ( span ​ ( { w } ) ) ⟂ \left(\text{span}(\{w\})\right)^{\perp} with ℝ N − 1 \mathbb{R}^{N-1} and noting that the orthogonal matrices on ℝ N − 1 \mathbb{R}^{N-1} act transitively on 𝕊 N − 2 \mathbb{S}^{N-2} , any matrix in ℝ N × N \mathbb{R}^{N\times N} that fixes w w and acts as an orthogonal matrix on ( span ​ ( { w } ) ) ⟂ ≅ ℝ N − 1 \left(\text{span}(\{w\})\right)^{\perp}\cong\mathbb{R}^{N-1} that shifts w ⟂ w_{\perp} will suffice. For such a matrix U 0 U_{0} , this would mean that U 0 ​ w ⟂ ≠ w ⟂ U_{0}w_{\perp}\neq w_{\perp} . Consequently, we must have that w ⟂ = 0 w_{\perp}=0 . Thus, we have found that M ​ w = λ w ​ w Mw=\lambda_{w}w ; that is, for any unit vector w ∈ 𝕊 N − 1 w\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1} , there exists some λ w ∈ ℝ \lambda_{w}\in\mathbb{R} such that M ​ w = λ w ​ w Mw=\lambda_{w}w . In particular, every unit vector in ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{N} is an eigenvector of M M . Now, we leverage the fact that the group of orthogonal matrices on ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{N} acts transitively on 𝕊 N − 1 \mathbb{S}^{N-1} . In particular, for any unit vectors w 1 , w 2 ∈ 𝕊 N − 1 w_{1},w_{2}\in\mathbb{S}^{N-1} , there exists some orthogonal matrix U U such that U ​ w 1 = w 2 Uw_{1}=w_{2} . Then, λ w 2 ​ w 2 = M ​ w 2 = M ​ U ​ w 1 = U ​ M ​ w 1 = U ⁡ ( λ w 1 ​ w 1 ) = λ w 1 ​ w 2 . \lambda_{w_{2}}w_{2}=Mw_{2}=MUw_{1}=UMw_{1}=U(\lambda_{w_{1}}w_{1})=\lambda_{w_{1}}w_{2}. Consequently, we find that λ w 1 = λ w 2 \lambda_{w_{1}}=\lambda_{w_{2}} . Thus, every unit vector in ℝ N \mathbb{R}^{N} is an eigenvector of M M with the same eigenvalue, which implies that M M is a scalar multiple of I N I_{N} . (b) Because M ​ U = U ​ M MU=UM for all orthogonal matrices U U that fix v v , our argument from part (a) shows that M ​ v = λ v ​ v Mv=\lambda_{v}v , for some λ v ∈ ℝ \lambda_{v}\in\mathbb{R} . Observe also that transposing this identity yields U T ​ M T = M T ​ U T U^{T}M^{T}=M^{T}U^{T} for all orthogonal matrices U U that fix v v . Moreover, since U T U^{T} is the inverse of U U , U U fixing v v is equivalent to U T U^{T} fixing v v ; thus, we also have that U ​ M T = M T ​ U UM^{T}=M^{T}U for all orthogonal matrices U U fixing v v . Following the same argument as in (a) again yields M T ​ v = λ v ′ ​ v M^{T}v=\lambda_{v}^{\prime}v , for some λ v ′ ∈ ℝ \lambda_{v}^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R} . Now, consider any w ∈ W := ( span ​ ( { v } ) ) ⟂ w\in W:=\left(\text{span}(\{v\})\right)^{\perp} . Note then that for any orthogonal matrix U U that fixes v v , ⟨ U ​ w , v ⟩ = ⟨ U ​ w , U ​ v ⟩ = ⟨ w , v ⟩ = 0 \left\langle Uw,v\right\rangle=\left\langle Uw,Uv\right\rangle=\left\langle w,v\right\rangle=0 meaning that U ​ w ∈ W Uw\in W . Moreover, ⟨ M ​ w , v ⟩ = w T ​ M T ​ v = λ v ′ ​ w T ​ v = 0 \left\langle Mw,v\right\rangle=w^{T}M^{T}v=\lambda_{v}^{\prime}w^{T}v=0 meaning that M ​ w ∈ W Mw\in W as well. As a result, M M may be viewed as a block diagonal operator on span ​ ( { v } ) ⊕ W \text{span}(\{v\})\oplus W . In particular, the identity M ​ U = U ​ M MU=UM implies that M | W ​ U | W = U | W ​ M | W M|_{W}U|_{W}=U|_{W}M|_{W} for any orthogonal matrix U U that fixes v v ; furthermore, the set of such matrices corresponds to operators that fix span ​ ( { v } ) \text{span}(\{v\}) and act as any orthogonal matrix on W W . Thus, identifying W W with ℝ N − 1 \mathbb{R}^{N-1} , we have that M | W ​ V = V ​ M | W M|_{W}V=VM|_{W} for all orthogonal matrices V ∈ ℝ ( N − 1 ) × ( N − 1 ) V\in\mathbb{R}^{(N-1)\times(N-1)} . By part (a), this implies that M | W = λ 1 ​ I N | W M|_{W}=\lambda_{1}I_{N}|_{W} , for some λ 1 ∈ ℝ \lambda_{1}\in\mathbb{R} . Combining this result with the fact that M ​ v = λ v ​ v Mv=\lambda_{v}v and defining λ 2 := λ v − λ 1 \lambda_{2}:=\lambda_{v}-\lambda_{1} , we find that M = λ 1 ​ I N + λ 2 ​ v ​ v T M=\lambda_{1}I_{N}+\lambda_{2}vv^{T} . ∎

sections.heading: B.2 Results from Probability Theory
sections.text: Definition B.2 . For two sequences of random variables ( X n ) n ≥ 1 (X_{n})_{n\geq 1} and ( Y n ) n ≥ 1 (Y_{n})_{n\geq 1} , we say that X n ​ ∼ a.s. ​ Y n X_{n}\overset{\text{a.s.}}{\sim}Y_{n} if X n − Y n ​ ⟶ a.s. ​ 0 X_{n}-Y_{n}\overset{\text{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow}0 as n → ∞ n\to\infty . If X n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}x , then X n ​ ⟶ L p ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{p}}{\longrightarrow}x for all p ≥ 1 p\geq 1 . Moreover, if X n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}x and Y n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ y Y_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}y , then X n + Y n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ x + y X_{n}+Y_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}x+y and X n ​ Y n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ x ​ y X_{n}Y_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}xy . Finally, if X n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ 0 X_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}0 , then X n ​ Y n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ 0 X_{n}Y_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}0 as well. Proof. First, if X n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}x , then X n − x ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ 0 X_{n}-x\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}0 and so 𝔼 ⁡ [ | X n − x | p ] ≤ 𝔼 ​ [ ( X n − x ) 2 ] p / 2 → 0 \mathbb{E}[|X_{n}-x|^{p}]\leq\mathbb{E}\left[\left(X_{n}-x\right)^{2}\right]^{p/2}\to 0 for any 1 ≤ p < 2 1\leq p<2 . For p > 2 p>2 , we use the elementary interpolation inequality over L p L^{p} space (a consequence of Hölder’s inequality): there exists some θ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) \theta\in(0,1) such that 1 p = 1 − θ 2 + θ 2 ​ p \frac{1}{p}=\frac{1-\theta}{2}+\frac{\theta}{2p} , and for this θ \theta , ‖ X n − x ‖ L p ≤ ‖ X n − x ‖ L 2 1 − θ ​ ‖ X n − x ‖ L 2 ​ p θ . \left\lVert X_{n}-x\right\rVert_{L^{p}}\leq||X_{n}-x||_{L^{2}}^{1-\theta}||X_{n}-x||_{L^{2p}}^{\theta}. Since ‖ X n − x ‖ L 2 → 0 ||X_{n}-x||_{L^{2}}\to 0 by assumption and ‖ X n − x ‖ L 2 ​ p ||X_{n}-x||_{L^{2p}} is uniformly bounded (as X n X_{n} is moment controlled), it follows that ‖ X n − x ‖ L p → 0 \left\lVert X_{n}-x\right\rVert_{L^{p}}\to 0 , thus proving that X n ​ ⟶ L p ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{p}}{\longrightarrow}x when p > 2 p>2 as well. As a result, when X n X_{n} and Y n Y_{n} are both moment controlled, with X n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}x and Y n ​ ⟶ L 2 ​ y Y_{n}\overset{L^{2}}{\longrightarrow}y , then X n + Y n X_{n}+Y_{n} and X n ​ Y n X_{n}Y_{n} are also moment controlled (Prop. B.11 ). Moreover, using the triangle inequality, ‖ X n + Y n − ( x + y ) ‖ L 2 ≤ ‖ X n − x ‖ L 2 + ‖ Y n − y ‖ L 2 → 0 \left\lVert X_{n}+Y_{n}-(x+y)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\leq\left\lVert X_{n}-x\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+\left\lVert Y_{n}-y\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\to 0 ‖ X n ​ Y n − x ​ y ‖ L 2 = ‖ X n ​ ( Y n − y ) + y ⁡ ( X n − x ) ‖ L 2 ≤ ‖ X n ​ ( Y n − y ) ‖ L 2 + | y | ⋅ ‖ X n − x ‖ L 2 → 0 \left\lVert X_{n}Y_{n}-xy\right\rVert_{L^{2}}=\left\lVert X_{n}(Y_{n}-y)+y(X_{n}-x)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\leq\left\lVert X_{n}(Y_{n}-y)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}+|y|\cdot\left\lVert X_{n}-x\right\rVert_{L^{2}}\to 0 where we have noted that ‖ X n ​ ( Y n − y ) ‖ L 2 = 𝔼 ​ [ X n 2 ​ ( Y n − y ) 2 ] 1 / 2 ≤ 𝔼 ​ [ X n 4 ] 1 / 4 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ( Y n − y ) 4 ] 1 / 4 = ‖ X n ‖ L 4 ⋅ ‖ Y n − y ‖ L 4 \left\lVert X_{n}(Y_{n}-y)\right\rVert_{L^{2}}=\mathbb{E}\left[X_{n}^{2}(Y_{n}-y)^{2}\right]^{1/2}\leq\mathbb{E}\left[X_{n}^{4}\right]^{1/4}\mathbb{E}\left[(Y_{n}-y)^{4}\right]^{1/4}=\left\lVert X_{n}\right\rVert_{L^{4}}\cdot\left\lVert Y_{n}-y\right\rVert_{L^{4}} ≤ ( | x | + ‖ X n − x ‖ L 4 ) ⋅ ‖ Y n − y ‖ L 4 → 0 . \leq\left(|x|+\left\lVert X_{n}-x\right\rVert_{L^{4}}\right)\cdot\left\lVert Y_{n}-y\right\rVert_{L^{4}}\to 0. Here, we have applied the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and noted that X n ​ ⟶ L p ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{p}}{\longrightarrow}x and Y n ​ ⟶ L p ​ y Y_{n}\overset{L^{p}}{\longrightarrow}y for all p ≥ 1 p\geq 1 (e.g. p = 4 p=4 ). Suppose that ( X n ) n ≥ 1 (X_{n})_{n\geq 1} is a sequence of random variables such that X n ​ ⟶ ℙ ​ x X_{n}\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\longrightarrow}x , for some nonrandom constant x ∈ ℝ x\in\mathbb{R} , and that ( X n ) n ≥ 1 (X_{n})_{n\geq 1} is moment controlled. Because X n ​ ⟶ ℙ ​ x X_{n}\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\longrightarrow}x , it is the case that lim n → ∞ ℙ ⁡ ( | X n − x | > ϵ ) = 0 \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{P}(|X_{n}-x|>\epsilon)=0 for any fixed ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 . Here, we have noted that X n X_{n} is moment controlled and that X n ​ ⟶ ℙ ​ x X_{n}\overset{\mathbb{P}}{\longrightarrow}x . Thus, lim sup n → ∞ 𝔼 ⁡ [ | X n − x | p ] ≤ ϵ p \lim\sup_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[|X_{n}-x|^{p}\right]\leq\epsilon^{p} for any ϵ > 0 \epsilon>0 , implying that lim n → ∞ 𝔼 ⁡ [ | X n − x | p ] = 0 \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[|X_{n}-x|^{p}\right]=0 , i.e. X n ​ ⟶ L p ​ x X_{n}\overset{L^{p}}{\longrightarrow}x . ∎

For m , n ∈ ℤ + m,n\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} , let Z ∈ ℝ m × n Z\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} be a matrix such that Z i ​ j ​ ∼ iid ​ 𝒩 ​ ( 0 , 1 ) Z_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathcal{N}(0,1) for each 1 ≤ i ≤ m , 1 ≤ j ≤ n 1\leq i\leq m,\text{ }1\leq j\leq n . Note that W ′ := 1 n ​ Z ​ Z T W^{\prime}:=\frac{1}{n}ZZ^{T} is also a Wishart matrix, with aspect ratio m n \frac{m}{n} . Theorem B.18 (Marcenko-Pastur Theorem) . Fix some q ∈ ( 0 , ∞ ) q\in(0,\infty) , define increasing sequences ( n k ) k ≥ 1 (n_{k})_{k\geq 1} and ( m k ) k ≥ 1 (m_{k})_{k\geq 1} of integers such that lim k → ∞ n k m k = q \lim_{k\to\infty}\frac{n_{k}}{m_{k}}=q . For each k k , define μ k := 1 n k ​ ∑ i = 1 n k δ λ i ​ ( W k ) \mu_{k}:=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\delta_{\lambda_{i}(W_{k})} to be the empirical spectral distribution (ESD) of the eigenvalues of W k W_{k} . Then, as k → ∞ k\to\infty , μ k \mu_{k} weakly almost surely converges to a deterministic measure μ MP q \mu_{\text{MP}}^{q} known as the Marcenko-Pastur law. This means that for any bounded continuous function f : ℝ → ℝ f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} , 1 n k ​ ∑ i = 1 n k f ⁡ ( λ i ​ ( W k ) ) = μ k ​ ( f ) ​ ⟶ a.s. ​ μ ​ ( f ) = ∫ f ⁡ ( x ) ​ μ MP q ​ ( 𝑑 x ) . \frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}f(\lambda_{i}(W_{k}))=\mu_{k}(f)\overset{\text{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow}\mu(f)=\int f(x)\mu_{\text{MP}}^{q}(dx). Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.37834v1 [stat.ML] 27 Oct 2026 Investigating the Early Signatures of Feature Learning in Deep Linear Networks Shaunak Bhandarkar Email: shaunak@princeton.edu Affiliation: Princeton University Boris Hanin Email: bhanin@princeton.edu Affiliation: Princeton University October 27, 2026 Abstract Deep neural networks learn data-dependent features, a capacity widely credited for their empirical success. However, explicitly characterizing what features emerge — and when they improve generalization — is challenging, since training is nonlinear and nonconvex and the data is often anisotropic. Here, we give a closed-form account of feature learning for a deep linear network in a mean-field parameterization, trained by one gradient step from initialization on high-dimensional data carrying a low-dimensional (spiked) signal. In the infinite-width mean-field limit, one step updates each layer’s feature kernel by a target-aligned rank-one spike, amplified by both the learning rate and the layer depth. We next assess how these features impact prediction through kernel ridge regression (KRR), finding that KRR on the learned feature kernel yields scalar inflation of the KRR estimator at initialization — an “anti-shrinkage” mechanism that reinflates task-relevant directions suppressed by ridge, while also amplifying noise. To study when this inflation improves generalization, in the overparameterized proportional limit we derive closed-form expressions for the bias, variance, and generalization errors of these estimators in terms of key macroscopic parameters — notably the spike strength and spike-target alignment. Crucially, we find that a one-step generalization advantage vanishes for isotropic inputs and appears when both the spike strength and an effective signal-to-noise ratio are sufficiently large, demonstrating that a successful first gradient step both requires and benefits from low-dimensional task structure. 1 Introduction A defining trait of deep neural networks is their ability to learn data-dependent features within their internal layers [ 1 ] . This ability marks a salient departure from their predecessors — kernel models — which utilize a fixed set of features and only learn how to weight them: z ⁡ ( x , θ ) = ∑ j = 1 N W j ​ ϕ j ​ ( x ) z(x;\theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}W_{j}\phi_{j}(x) (1.1) Here, θ = ( W 1 , W 2 , … , W N ) \theta=(W_{1},W_{2},\dots,W_{N}) is a collection of regression weights and ϕ 1 , ϕ 2 , … , ϕ N \phi_{1},\phi_{2},\dots,\phi_{N} are basis functions that transform the input x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} into the features ( ϕ j ​ ( x ) ) 1 ≤ j ≤ N (\phi_{j}(x))_{1\leq j\leq N} , giving rise to a feature map x ↦ ( ϕ 1 ​ ( x ) , … , ϕ N ​ ( x ) ) x\mapsto(\phi_{1}(x),\dots,\phi_{N}(x)) . A kernel model learns the W j W_{j} while holding this map fixed; a deep network additionally adapts the map to the data through training. This process of feature learning is widely credited for the empirical success of deep networks [ 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] , yet it is precisely what places them outside the reach of kernel theory. We therefore ask: what data-dependent features does a deep neural network learn, and when do such features generalize better than fixed, data-independent ones? Answers to these questions are complicated by two issues. First, the learning dynamics of deep neural networks are nonlinear and nonconvex, making closed-form descriptions of feature learning limited. A large body of work addresses this issue by passing to an infinite-width limit ( N → ∞ N\to\infty ), in which aspects of the network dynamics collapse onto deterministic objects. The μ ​ P \mu P [ 6 ] and mean-field [ 7 ] network parameterizations support stable feature learning in this limit, and have been used to analyze the training dynamics and convergence properties of deep networks [ 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 ] . Within these descriptions, the dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) [ 12 , 13 ] characterizes the full training trajectory in terms of a reduced set of deterministically evolving kernel order parameters, which include the network’s feature kernels at each layer. This analysis is powerful, but it characterizes feature learning implicitly through self-consistent equations for order parameters, rather than explicitly computing the features learned under gradient descent. Additionally, the DMFT typically involves fixing the training dataset [ 12 , 14 , 15 , 16 ] , leaving open settings in which the number of data points n n and data dimension D D grow in addition to the width N N (which [ 16 ] explores for deep linear networks). See Appendix A for more details. The second issue is that the usefulness of any learned features depends on the underlying data distribution. While prior theoretical approaches often use isotropic inputs [ 1 , 17 , 18 , 19 , 20 ] , real-world data often contains low-dimensional structure embedded in otherwise high-dimensional observations [ 21 , 22 ] . A canonical model for studying such structure is a spiked matrix model [ 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 ] , in which a rank-one signal is embedded in high-dimensional noise. For regression tasks, this model is governed by two key parameters: the spike strength ( γ ≥ 0 \gamma\geq 0 ) of this rank-one signal, and the spike-target alignment ( ρ ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] \rho\in[-1,1] ) between the signal and ground truth regression directions. Altogether, inputs are sampled as x i ​ ∼ iid ​ N ​ ( 0 , I D + γ ​ v ​ v T ) x_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,I_{D}+\gamma vv^{T}) and targets as y i = 1 D ​ w ⋆ T ​ x i + ϵ i y_{i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}w_{\star}^{T}x_{i}+\epsilon_{i} , with ϵ i ​ ∼ iid ​ N ​ ( 0 , σ 2 ) \epsilon_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^{2}) and w ⋆ w_{\star} fixed so that 1 D ​ w ⋆ T ​ v = ρ \frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}w_{\star}^{T}v=\rho . In light of these issues, here we develop a simplified framework for describing feature learning and when it is useful, making three key modeling choices that afford closed-form analysis while preserving the phenomenon of interest. First, we study deep linear networks with L ≥ 1 L\geq 1 layers and width N N , in a mean-field parameterization, for which optimization remains nonlinear, nonconvex, as well as genuinely depth-dependent [ 25 , 26 ] . Second, for a fixed dataset of D D -dimensional inputs X = [ x 1 , … , x n ] ∈ ℝ D × n X=[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times n} and scalar targets y = [ y 1 , … , y n ] ∈ ℝ n y=[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n} , we take a single gradient descent (GD) step with step size η \eta on the empirical mean squared error loss from initialization. As a result, writing θ t \theta_{t} for the network’s weights after t t steps of GD ( t ∈ { 0 , 1 } t\in\{0,1\} ), this approach allows us to exactly calculate each layer’s feature kernel Φ t ℓ := ( h ℓ ​ ( x i , θ t ) ⋅ h ℓ ​ ( x j , θ t ) N ) 1 ≤ i , j ≤ n ∈ ℝ n × n , 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ L , \Phi^{\ell}_{t}:=\left(\frac{h^{\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{t})\cdot h^{\ell}(x_{j};\theta_{t})}{N}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n},\hskip 23.49976pt1\leq\ell\leq L, (1.2) in the limit of N → ∞ N\to\infty (with n n and D D fixed), both before and after one step, and to compare it with the baseline input kernel K x := X T ​ X D ∈ ℝ n × n K_{x}:=\frac{X^{T}X}{D}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} . Here, h ℓ ​ ( x , θ ) ∈ ℝ N h^{\ell}(x;\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{N} denotes the layer- ℓ \ell representation of the input x ∈ ℝ D x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} . Third, to study when the features given by the limiting layer- ℓ \ell one-step feature kernel are useful, we sample data from a spiked matrix model and subsequently take n , D → ∞ n,D\to\infty ; this enables us to compute (in closed-form) the generalization error arising from these features under kernel ridge regression (for any ridge strength λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 ) in the overparameterized proportional limit n / D → ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) n/D\to\psi\in(0,1) , and to identify settings of γ \gamma and ρ \rho that lead to better generalization after one step. Together, these choices allow us to discover how one gradient step updates the layer- ℓ \ell feature kernel, how this change propagates to the resulting kernel ridge estimator, and for which data distributions this update lowers the generalization error. Ultimately, we find that one gradient step within a deep linear network causes each of its layers to acquire a target-aligned low-rank spike, setting it up to improve generalization for data distributions with target-aligned low-dimensional structure (i.e. γ \gamma and ρ 2 / σ 2 \rho^{2}/\sigma^{2} are sufficiently large), and to fail to do so if this structure is missing (Fig. 1 ). Our approach is reminiscent of the one-step analysis of Ba et al. (2022) [ 19 ] , in which one gradient step in a nonlinear network with one hidden layer ( L = 1 L=1 ) causes the first-layer weights to acquire a target-aligned rank-one spike. Moreover, ridge regression on the updated hidden-state activations leads to meaningful improvement in generalization for a sufficiently large step. We find similar results in our work (see our contributions below). Unlike Ba et al., however, we do not consider nonlinearities. Nonetheless, this simplification precisely allows us to capture (in closed-form) feature learning in deeper networks ( L > 1 ) (L>1) and isolate the role of structure in the data in shaping a generalization advantage. 1.1 Our Contributions Our core findings and analyses can be summarized as follows. 1. One step imprints a target-aligned rank-one spike on every feature kernel, amplified by learning rate and depth. For a fixed dataset { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 n \left\{(x_{i},y_{i})\right\}_{i=1}^{n} , let y = [ y 1 , … , y n ] ∈ ℝ n y=[y_{1},\dots,y_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{n} denote the stacked targets. Then, as N → ∞ N\to\infty , the layer- ℓ \ell feature kernel Φ ℓ \Phi^{\ell} concentrates to the input kernel K x K_{x} at initialization and, after one GD step, to K feat ℓ := K x + η 2 ​ d ℓ n 2 ​ K x ​ y ​ y T ​ K x K_{\feat}^{\ell}:=K_{x}+\frac{\eta^{2}d_{\ell}}{n^{2}}K_{x}yy^{T}K_{x} (1.3) where d ℓ := ℓ ​ ( ℓ + 1 ) ​ ( 2 ​ ℓ + 1 ) 6 d_{\ell}:=\frac{\ell(\ell+1)(2\ell+1)}{6} (Thm. 3.1 ; see Fig. 2 ). Crucially, the strength of this update grows with the step size η \eta and with the layer index ℓ \ell . Thus, for a fixed step size, feature evolution after one step is more dramatic in deeper layers. 2. One step of feature learning inflates estimation. Letting f ^ λ ; feat \hat{f}_{\lambda;\feat} and f ^ λ ; init \hat{f}_{\lambda;\init} denote the kernel ridge regression (KRR) estimators (with fixed ridge strength λ ≥ 0 \lambda\geq 0 ) arising from K feat ℓ K_{\feat}^{\ell} and K x K_{x} , respectively, we find that f ^ λ ; feat ​ ( x ) = c λ ​ f ^ λ ; init ​ ( x ) ∀ x ∈ ℝ D \hat{f}_{\lambda;\feat}(x)=c_{\lambda}\hat{f}_{\lambda;\init}(x)\hskip 23.49976pt\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^{D} (1.4) where c λ ≥ 1 c_{\lambda}\geq 1 is a ridge- and data-dependent constant that uniformly inflates estimation (Prop. 3.2 ); inflation vanishes at λ = 0 \lambda=0 ( c λ = 1 c_{\lambda}=1 ). Thus, genuine inflation requires nonzero ridge and either performing a large gradient step — reminiscent of [ 19 ] — or sufficient depth. Since a one-step KRR estimator is pinned by ( λ , k ℓ ) (\lambda,k_{\ell}) , we write it as f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} throughout, with k ℓ = 0 k_{\ell}=0 recovering the baseline ridge estimator f ^ λ ; init \hat{f}_{\lambda;\init} . 3. For data coming from a spiked population model, we derive and analyze closed-form asymptotic formulas for bias, variance, and generalization error. In the proportional limit n / D → ψ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ) n/D\to\psi\in(0,1) and where the task is noisy linear regression ( y i = 1 D w ⋆ T x i + ϵ i , ϵ i ∼ iid N ( 0 , σ 2 ) ) \left(y_{i}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{D}}w_{\star}^{T}x_{i}+\epsilon_{i},\text{ }\epsilon_{i}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}N(0,\sigma^{2})\right) , we derive these exact formulas for f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} (Thm. 4.3 ; see Fig. 4 ). We decompose the generalization error into bias , which measures how well the average predictor fits the targets, and variance , which measures the estimator’s sensitivity to the specific dataset. Since all estimators coincide when λ = 0 \lambda=0 , we ask how feature learning affects bias and variance when mild ridge is added (Prop. 4.4 ; Fig. 5 ): (A) To first order in λ \lambda around λ = 0 \lambda=0 , the bias of the baseline estimator f ^ λ ; 0 \hat{f}_{\lambda;0} increases and its variance decreases. (B) To first order in λ \lambda around λ = 0 \lambda=0 , the effect of adding feature learning ( 0 < k ℓ = Θ D ​ ( 1 ) 0<k_{\ell}=\Theta_{D}(1) ) is to decrease the bias (of f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} ) relative to that of f ^ λ ; 0 \hat{f}_{\lambda;0} , and to increase the variance (of f ^ λ ; k ℓ \hat{f}_{\lambda;k_{\ell}} ) relative to that of f ^ λ ; 0 \hat{f}_{\lambda;0} . Altogether, ridge and feature learning act as opposing forces along the bias-variance axis. Intuitively, ridge alone shrinks the estimator, increasing bias, but improves robustness to noise in the dataset, decreasing variance. Adding feature learning-induced uniform inflation corrects shrinkage on average at the cost of amplifying noise along task-irrelevant directions. The question is when this bias-for-variance trade is worth making. 4. A feature learning advantage exists when the data carries a sufficiently strong, target-aligned spike, and vanishes in the absence of a spike or target-alignment (see Fig. 1 ) . Collectively, these results resemble a deep linear network-based analog of the famous BBP phase transition [ 24 , 27 ] : the “spiked” one-step kernel meaningfully picks up the “spike” in the data once the spike strength and SNR are sufficiently large. 1.2 Related Works Deep linear networks. Despite their lack of nonlinearities, deep linear networks possess a nonconvex loss landscape [ 28 ] and depth-dependent training dynamics [ 25 , 29 ] , making them an analytically tractable testbed for theories of learning [ 30 , 12 , 31 , 32 ] . Notably, Saxe et al. (2014) [ 25 ] show that when weights are suitably “decoupled”, modes of the input–output correlation are acquired sequentially in order of their singular values, so that depth gives rise to “stage-like” transitions in learning. Closer to our question, Atanasov et al. (2022) [ 33 ] show that at small initialization a deep linear network’s neural tangent kernel (NTK) can align with the target early in training. In a similar vein, we make the earliest such alignment explicit: after a single step, each layer’s feature kernel acquires a target-aligned rank-one component. One-step analyses. A key approach for explicitly characterizing the features a network acquires is to study the features learned after a single GD step from initialization. For two-layer nonlinear networks, Ba et al. (2022) [ 19 ] show that one GD step imprints a rank-one “spike” on the first-layer weights that aligns with the linear component of the target, and that ridge regression on the resulting features can strictly improve generalization over kernel estimators with no learned features once the step size is large enough. Subsequent work refines this picture: larger learning-rate scalings can imprint multiple spikes, each capturing a higher-order component of the target [ 34 ] ; the one-GD-step network can be mapped to a spiked random features model, for which test error asymptotics may be derived [ 35 ] ; and learning multi-index targets requires characteristic batch sizes and numbers of GD steps [ 20 ] . These analyses treat two-layer nonlinear networks with isotropic inputs, and typically express the generalization error through self-consistent equations that must be solved numerically. In this paper, we study linear networks but account for depth and a particular class of anisotropic inputs, and we carry out our analyses in closed form. Spiked matrix models. The spiked population model we study stems from Johnstone (2001) [ 23 ] , and its defining feature is the BBP transition [ 24 ] : the top sample eigenvalue separates from the bulk only once the spike strength exceeds a critical value set by the aspect ratio. Using this model, prior work has shown that feature learning can exploit a spike, a property that depends both on the spike strength and the spike-target alignment [ 21 , 22 ] . In this paper, we make this dependence quantitative for a deep linear network. High-dimensional ridge regression. Ridge regularization classically serves to shrink estimation, mitigating overfitting in order to lower test error [ 36 ] . Using tools from random matrix theory — notably the Marcenko–Pastur law — prior work has derived asymptotics for the generalization error of ridge regression in the proportional regime and characterized the optimal ridge strength [ 37 ] . However, this shrinkage prescription can fail for heavily overparameterized settings ( D ≫ n D\gg n ) in which the population covariance is anisotropic and the true regression direction is aligned with its top eigendirections [ 38 ] . For example, for a spiked covariance, the optimal ridge strength can even be negative [ 39 ] . More recently, Freeman (2025) [ 40 ] shows that scalar inflation of the minimum ℓ 2 \ell_{2} -norm interpolator ( λ = 0 \lambda=0 ) lowers the generalization error for sufficiently anisotropic covariances when D ≫ n D\gg n . These ideas challenge the classical wisdom that shrinkage enhances prediction, suggesting that inflating estimation can improve test error in certain cases. In this paper, we arrive at inflation from a different angle. Rather than being prescribed, the inflation factor c λ c_{\lambda} is produced by one GD step; in effect, the deep linear network discovers an anti-shrinkage correction on its own. 2 Problem Setup Notation.
